newsitem.title: UK: Ford averts British strike threat with union deal.
newsitem.headline: Ford averts British strike threat with union deal.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. averted a possible national strike by British auto workers Friday by clinching a deal with trade unions to secure the future of its Halewood plant in northwest England.
A union statement said the agreement secured jobs and guaranteed job security both at Halewood in Liverpool and throughout the company's other British plants.
Roger Butler of the Amalgamated Engineers and Electricians Unions (AEEU) hailed the breakthrough as "a major victory for Ford workers."

The deal came after two days of talks between Ford's European head Jac Nasser and union leaders. These were a last ditch effort by the workers to try to save 1,300 jobs after Ford's decision last month to move production of its new Escort model to Continental Europe.
Ford said later that 980 employees would be let go, rather than the originally planned 1,300.
Production of the Escort will still switch to Germany and Spain but union leaders said mainstream models will continue to be made at Halewood.
A threat of a strike by all Ford workers in Britain was called off after the deal. Halewood workers will vote on the agreement next week.
Failure of the talks could have led to a strike by up to 20,000 Ford production line workers, just ahead of a British election which must be called by May.
Earlier one union official outlined the points put forward to the Ford management in the talks.

"Our arguments are that there is no economic reason for this. The plant has increased productivity, labour costs are down and we have met all our targets. The only reason for moving the jobs to the Continent is that the cost of sacking (firing) people in Britain is cheaper."
Unions have claimed it is less expensive to cut jobs in Britain because the government has opted out of the European Union's Social Chapter which gives greater protection to employees.

The move to cut jobs was triggered by heavy losses in Ford's European division due to sluggish regional demand, particularly in the French and German markets which make up around 40 percent of Ford's European sales according to industry analyst LMC International.
The Big Three automaker has also been trying to negotiate an increased subsidy from the British government to secure the future of the plant.
